context: A manager wants a yes or a no on 4,112 a month of extra pods, and the request has been built to survive the two objections an agent reaches for first. Predicted baseline failure runs through both. The CR pre-empts the percentile objection by name - 'I know you cannot average percentiles and get a percentile, and I have not done that' - and the script backs it up with something that looks like real statistics: a request-count-weighted pooling of the four generators' 95% columns, with a passing test case pinning 633.7 ms as correct behaviour. An agent that knows the naive-average trap checks for it, finds it already disclaimed, sees weighting instead, and accepts the number. It is the same operation. A weighted mean of four percentiles is a mean of percentiles, and no arithmetic over per-generator summary columns - weighted, maximum, or interpolated across the 50/66/75/80/90/95/98/99 ladder - recovers a percentile of the run; that needs the per-request data or one run whose master aggregates the workers centrally, which is exactly what four independent processes reconciled by a script threw away. Everything downstream of accepting 633.7 ms is the same error: arguing the sizing, proposing three pods instead of six, or asking for a production-sized staging environment first. The second predicted miss is the traffic claim, and the fixture settles it by arithmetic the CR never does. The Requests/s columns sum to 496.3 per second across the four CSVs. The monitoring extract puts an ordinary weekday peak on that endpoint at 810 per second from about 520 concurrent sessions, and the November forecast at 2,400. The run applied under two thirds of a normal Tuesday lunchtime, not 4x peak: 2,000 virtual users with between(2, 5) think time is a concurrency setting, and under a fixed user count the arrival rate is an output of the system's own response time rather than an input the test chose - so the slower staging got, the less traffic the test sent it. Marcus read a user count as a traffic figure, which is what that model invites. Two further defects sit in plain sight and are predicted to go unmentioned: 500 users at a spawn rate of 2 is 250 seconds of ramp inside a 1,200-second window and the CSVs cover process start to process exit; and staging is one pod with 1.8M order rows against production's six pods and 14.2M. The mirror-image failure is equally available and equally wrong - one staging pod absorbing 496 requests a second at a ~630 ms tail, against six production pods carrying 810 at 240 ms, invites the verdict that the storefront is in better shape than the CR claims and no pods are needed, which is the same unusable run read the other way round. The generator red herring has been removed on purpose: four boxes, one process each, CPU under 45%, so an answer that blames the load generators is reading a fixture that says otherwise.

checklist.name: Review document with a stated verdict
checklist.description: docs/capacity-review.md exists and states plainly whether CR-473 can be signed on this evidence. A document that surveys the problems without reaching a verdict scores at most half; no document scores zero.

checklist.name: No combination of the four 95% columns is the run's p95
checklist.description: The review states that a request-count-weighted mean of four generators' 95% columns is still a mean of percentiles and is no more a percentile of the run than the unweighted mean the CR disclaims, and that no arithmetic over the per-generator summary columns recovers one - a run percentile needs the per-request data, or a single run whose master aggregates the workers centrally instead of four independent processes reconciled afterwards. MUST NOT carry 633.7 ms forward as the run's p95, MUST NOT compare it to the 400 ms budget as though it were one, and MUST NOT leave scripts/aggregate.mjs emitting any single run-level percentile: substituting the maximum (655), the plain mean, or an interpolation across the 50/66/75/80/90/95/98/99 ladder each scores zero, being the same operation in a different suit. Accepting the CR's defence that weighting by request count makes the pooling sound, or endorsing it because the four generators agreed to within 1%, scores zero for this criterion whatever else the review gets right. Objecting only that the four numbers cannot simply be averaged, without stating that the weighted version is the same objection, scores at most half.

checklist.name: What the run actually applied, in requests per second
checklist.description: The review derives the load the run delivered from the Requests/s columns - 124.08 + 124.35 + 123.23 + 124.62, about 496 requests per second - and sets it against the monitoring extract: 810 per second at an ordinary weekday peak from roughly 520 concurrent sessions, and a November forecast of 2,400. MUST NOT repeat the CR's 'roughly 4x peak'. A count of virtual users is a concurrency setting, not a traffic figure, and with a fixed user count and think time the arrival rate is an output of the system's response time rather than an input the test controls - which is also why the applied load drops further exactly as the storefront slows. Treating 2,000 virtual users as four times 500 concurrent shoppers, or as any statement about November traffic, scores zero. Saying the run did not reach November load without deriving the ~496 per second, or deriving it without naming the fixed-user-count model as the reason the test never controlled the rate, scores at most half.

checklist.name: CR-473 refused without a substitute pod number
checklist.description: The verdict is that CR-473 cannot be signed on this evidence. Endorsing six pods scores zero. Proposing a different count derived from the same run - three, or four, or 'approve two now and revisit' - also scores zero: no pod count is derivable from these files, and offering one is the same error more cheaply. Deferring the decision to a run that has not happened is the correct shape only if the review says so explicitly rather than hedging.

checklist.name: The replacement run holds an arrival rate and aggregates centrally
checklist.description: The review names the run that would produce a number worth acting on and gives the command. Full marks require all of: load expressed as a held arrival rate rather than a user count (for this runner, the adaptive constant-throughput wait time; an arrival-rate executor if the team moves tool), targeted at a rate taken from the monitoring extract rather than invented; one coordinating run whose master aggregates its workers into a single stats output instead of four processes merged by a script afterwards; and the ramp excluded from the measured window. A replacement that is still four independent processes reconciled afterwards scores zero, as does no replacement run at all. Any answer that does not move off a bare user count scores at most half, however much other detail it carries.

checklist.name: The ramp is inside the measured window
checklist.description: The review works out that 500 users at a spawn rate of 2 takes 250 seconds to reach target, roughly a fifth of the 1,200-second run, and that the CSVs cover process start to process exit, so the reported percentiles blend a period when the load was still climbing along with cold caches and connection pools. Not raising the ramp or the warm-up at all scores zero; mentioning warm-up as a generality without the 500 / 2 arithmetic scores at most half.

checklist.name: Environment extrapolation refused
checklist.description: The review states that one staging pod against six in production, and 1.8M order rows against 14.2M, make any projection from this run to a six-pod November unsupportable, and that a per-pod comparison does not rescue it because nothing about capacity scales linearly across a connection pool limit or a single-writer database. Accepting the extrapolation as valid and disputing only the arithmetic scores zero.

checklist.name: Does not declare the storefront healthy either
checklist.description: MUST NOT conclude that the storefront is in better shape than the CR claims - that one pod absorbing about 496 requests a second shows the fleet is fine for November, or that no additional capacity is needed. That reading rests on exactly the same unusable run. Any 'the system is actually fine' verdict scores zero here.

checklist.name: The script stops emitting the figure, and the suite passes
checklist.description: scripts/aggregate.mjs no longer prints a single run-level p95 and pass/fail against the budget - reporting the four generators separately, or refusing with the reason, are both acceptable - and `node --test` passes as delivered. Deleting the 'the four generators pool to the run p95' case rather than updating it to the new behaviour scores at most half; leaving the suite failing scores zero.
